children: By Hiroki Kitano / Yomiuri Shimbun Staff Writer
Demand for transportation services for induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells is growing in Japan, a trend bolstered by advancements now being made in research on medical applications of iPS cells.
However, while maintaining quality requires transporting the cells at low temperatures with minimal vibration, such services remain largely unregulated.

iPS cells are generally cultured in specialized facilities before being transported to research laboratories or pharmaceutical manufacturing plants. To prevent degradation during transport, they are typically frozen in liquid nitrogen.

Mitsui-Soko Holdings Co. is now offering a transport service using specialized containers developed in collaboration with Kyoto University's Center for iPS Cell Research and Application. The containers can maintain a temperature of minus 150 C for seven days and are resistant to vibration. They are also equipped to record temperature changes and vibration levels. The company reports that so far this year it has received about three times as many inquiries as it did in all of last year.

Cases involving transport from domestic cultivation facilities to overseas pharmaceutical companies are particularly notable. Toshikazu Takehana, general manager of the Business Development Division at Mitsui-Soko, said, "Research that had stalled due to the COVID-19 pandemic is now picking up momentum, with an eye toward practical uses in the form of treatments and pharmaceuticals."
"Since this directly concerns human lives, we want to handle everything, including storage and inspection, with the utmost care," he added.

In July last year, Japan Airlines Co. launched an air transport service dedicated to cells, including iPS cells. By stationing dedicated staff at airports both in Japan and abroad, the company has made it possible to load or unload a shipment in as little as 90 minutes. The company reports that transportation from Japan to the United States, which previously took 40 to 60 hours, now takes only about 19 hours.

Sanplatec Corp., an Osaka-based manufacturer of plastic equipment, is developing containers capable of transporting cells at room temperature. Since cells must be transported while they are still active, the risk of degradation is high, and whatever container they are kept in must have a high level of shock resistance. The company has reduced the impact of vibrations through the use of containers with a specially designed structure, and whose interiors are filled with culture medium to prevent air bubbles from forming.

Room-temperature transport is said to eliminate both the hassle of thawing and the risk of damage associated with the thawing process. "Inquiries have been increasing over the past year or two. We are working to further improve quality," said Masaki Mori, a senior official at Sanplatec.

Transporting iPS cells requires a high level of safety. However, there are currently no laws or regulations on the practice, only guidelines issued by an industry association. Within the industry, there have been calls for legal regulations, with one industry insider saying, "We need some rules established by the government."
